text: Intensive means packed with a huge amount of effort and attention. Here it describes parents who put lots of time and money into their children's lessons and activities.
To bankroll something is to pay for it, usually all of it. Here parents are paying for lessons, camps, and tutors so their children can get ahead.
To stagnate is to stop growing or improving and just stay the same, like a pond with no moving water. Here the chance that kids do better than their parents has stopped rising.
A preserve is something that belongs to only one group, like a private club. The title says intensive parenting is no longer only for the rich.
Wealthy means having a lot of money. It is another word for rich.
Offspring means a person's children. The word is often used for the young of animals too.
Edification means teaching someone so that their mind or character improves. Here it means paying for lessons that help kids learn and grow.
A competition is a contest where people try to do better than each other. Here families compete for limited spots at schools and good jobs.
To splash out means to spend a lot of money, often more than you normally would. Here parents in Asia are spending freely on their children's schooling.
Socioeconomic describes a person's place in society based on money, education, and job. Socioeconomic divides are the gaps between richer and poorer groups.
A divide is a gap that separates groups. Here the divides are the differences between rich and poor families.
Tykes is a playful word for small children.
Toddlers are very young children, around one to three years old, who are just learning to walk and talk.
A chauffeur is a driver. To chauffeur children means to drive them from place to place, like parents taking kids to practices.
To confer is to talk with someone to share ideas or make a decision. Here parents talk with coaches.
Cumulative means added up over time. A cumulative rate is the total change over several years, not just one.
Inflation is when prices across a whole economy rise over time, so the same money buys less. Here sports costs grew twice as fast as normal price rises.
A quintile is one fifth of a group. The lowest income quintile means the poorest fifth of families.
A quartile is one quarter of a group. The lowest quartile means the poorest quarter of families.
Tutoring is extra one-on-one or small-group teaching, often paid for, outside regular school. In some countries it is called tuition.
An obsession is something you think about or focus on all the time. Here tutoring has been the thing many parents in Asia care most about.
The OECD is a club of mostly rich countries that collects facts and figures about their economies and schools.
Disposable income is the money a family has left to spend or save after taxes are paid.
A household is all the people who live together in one home. Household spending is what that family spends.
Urban means having to do with cities and towns, the opposite of rural.
Pupils are students who go to school. The word is common in British writing.
The Sutton Trust is a British charity that works to help children from poorer families do well at school.
A charity is a group that works to help people or a cause, rather than to make a profit.
State-educated means taught in a public school paid for by the government, not a private school.
If a gap has narrowed, it has gotten smaller. Here the difference between poor and rich students who get tutoring is shrinking.
State-funded means paid for by the government with public money.
Youngsters are young people, such as children and teenagers.
Soft virtues are gentle good qualities like independence and imagination. They are the opposite of hard skills you can test, such as exam scores.
Independence is being able to think and act on your own without constant help from others.
If something is perceived a certain way, that is how people see it, even if it is not exactly true.
To instil a quality is to slowly teach it so it becomes part of a person, like teaching hard work from a young age.
A toll is a cost or harm that builds up. The financial toll is the money that families have to give up.
Eye-watering describes something, often a price, that is so big it shocks you.
A lifetime is the whole time a person lives. Lifetime educational investment is all the money spent on a person's learning.
Social mobility is how easily people can move up or down in money and success compared with their parents. Here the extra spending has not made that easier.
Translating usually means changing words into another language. Here it means turning one thing into another: money spent into better chances in life.
To collapse is to fall down suddenly. Here the chance of kids doing better than their parents dropped sharply in Singapore and South Korea.
When a school admits students, it lets them in. Harvard admits only a small share of those who apply.
Applicants are people who ask for a place at a school or job.
Rural means having to do with the countryside and farms, not cities.
A graduate is someone who has finished a university degree. A non-graduate family is one where the parents did not finish university.
The college earnings premium is the extra pay a person with a degree gets compared with someone without one.
Percentage points measure the gap between two percentages. Going from 20% to 30% is a rise of ten percentage points.
A think-tank is a group of experts who study problems and suggest ideas.
Free school meals are lunches that schools give for free to children from low-income families. In Britain they are used to tell who is poor.
To have the edge is to have a small advantage over others. Rich parents still have the edge in the competition for good futures.
